newsitem.title: MONACO: RALLYING-TURINI NIGHT ENDS AS NEW ERA DAWNS.
newsitem.headline: RALLYING-TURINI NIGHT ENDS AS NEW ERA DAWNS.

text.p: There will be no more Turini nights in Monte Carlo, where a new era for international rallying dawns on Sunday with the start of the 1997 world championship.

A revolution in format and rules aimed at making the sport more exciting has forced the organisers of the winter classic to drop the traditional night finale over the Turini pass in the mountains overlooking the principality.

There will be 14 rounds this season compared to nine last year and they will be shorter as rally chiefs want to turn the championship into a global series capable of capturing attention from the public and the media.
This means the likes of world champion Tommi Makinen of Finland and Britain's Colin McRae will not converge on Monte Carlo from several European cities, as they did in previous years.

The rally, which was left out of the world championship last year, will effectively start from the tiny principality on Sunday and end there on Wednesday after a final timed stage using a portion of the Monaco Grand Prix circuit.
The new rules, meant to cut costs and minimise the strain on top drivers, who have to contest every round, will also introduce different cars.
In a way they are more closely linked to ordinary road cars, as they must be part of a production run of at least 25,000, compared to a requirement of only 2,500 for the former group A cars.

But the new, 'world rally cars' (WRC), are improved in some sections, as they have only to belong to a 'family' of the same car which sells more than 25,000 each year. The group A cars had to be identical to the road-going models.
Ironically, the WRCs bear an aggressive look which evokes the extremely powerful but dangerous group B prototypes which were banned in the late 1980s.

But Ford Motorsport technical director Philip Dunabin insisted the new cars, based on a two-litre, turbo-charged, four-wheel drive mid-sized family saloon with a minimum weight of 1230 kgs, are much safer.
"They may look like group B cars but they are certainly not group B cars," he said. "They are improved, safer and more reliable group A cars."
Three constructors, world champions Mitsubishi, Subaru and Ford, will launch new WRCs this season and will battle it out with group A cars, still able to enter but probably a little slower.
The race for the title should be decided between those three manufacturers, who will rely on the world's finest drivers.
Makinen, in his Mitsubishi Lancer Evolution 4, McRae, in his Subaru Impreza WRC, and Spaniard Carlos Sainz, in his Ford Escort WRC, should be ahead of the rest of the field.

In Monte Carlo, where the race should be tricky this year with wintry conditions and roads covered with ice and snow, experience is a key-factor and four times winner Didier Auriol of France will be one to watch, even if his privately-entered, group A Ford sounds slightly less competitive.
"I'm confident," said Auriol, the 1994 world champion. "I don't think the car will be a lot slower than the WRCs and I really believe I stand a chance."
